title: Leaders in Transition: What Matters Most
author: Mueller, Kurt
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership, July 31, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller argues that leadership transitions fail not because leaders lack competence but because they confuse two distinct dimensions of the transition: what the change means to them personally, and what the new situation actually requires from them professionally. He proposes a five-step framework: define what actually changed specifically; identify what the transition means personally; read the situational demand carefully; identify the specific capability gap; and apply the new capability to a concrete leadership challenge. Mueller illustrates the framework with Paul, a manager promoted after a reorganisation who confused a need for personal confidence with the professional need for cross-functional influence skills. The article argues that leadership development only works when the capability being developed is tied to an actual situational demand rather than a generalised aspiration. It concludes that transitions are diagnostic tools — they surface exactly which capabilities need to develop next.
points: When personal meaning and situational requirements get blended together in a leadership transition, a manageable challenge can quickly feel much larger and more threatening.

Define what actually changed — be specific, not vague: did decision authority change? Did expectations increase? Did a key stakeholder leave? Clarity about the change itself reduces unnecessary anxiety.
Leadership development only works when the capability being developed is tied to an actual situational demand rather than a generalised aspiration or vague feeling of inadequacy.
Before deciding what you need to develop, examine what the new situation specifically requires — who the critical stakeholders are, what outcomes matter most, and what decisions are now yours alone.
Paul's real development need was not simply becoming more confident — it was building the cross-functional influence skills that his specific new situation actually demanded.
quotes: Identify the capability gap Only now ask, “What do I need to develop?” You may discover that the answer is better stakeholder communication, greater decisiveness, delegation, political awareness, conflict management, or something else entirely.

It became clear that the development need was not simply “becoming more confident.” This is why we worked instead on building alignment without relying on positional authority.
But you do need to periodically ask whether the way you are leading still fits the situation you are now in through both personal fulfillment and meeting expectations.
The second turns your attention outward toward stakeholders, outcomes, constraints, decisions, and the leadership behaviors the situation actually demands.
Situationally, however, the bigger requirement was coordinating across functions and influencing stakeholders who no longer report directly to the him.
This allowed us to focus on development that helps create the impact that Paul was looking for and the confidence that followed.
